newsitem.title: USA: Judge won't consider harm to Food Lion yet.
newsitem.headline: Judge won't consider harm to Food Lion yet.

text.p: U.S. District Court Judge Carlton Tilley sent the jury from the courtroom and told lawyers they could not probe damages or harm to Food Lion Inc's reputation from an ABC Television program until a ruling was made in the liability aspect of the trial. Tilley still has not ruled on whether Food Lion can claim damages. "I will not allow you to get into loss of sales," the judge said. "I will hear you at an appropriate time." Testimony began in Food Lion's suit against Walt Disney Co's ABC Television Tuesday, with the grocer's human resources vice-president Eugene McKinley describing how ABC producers allegedly applied for Food Lion jobs in a deceptive manner. McKinley said nowhere on the application did two producers indicate they had another full time job or that ABC was their employer. "(Applications) should be filled out accurately and completely," he told jurors. McKinley said the company discourages full time employees from working for another company because of the varying work schedules of a grocery store worker. Food Lion filed a lawsuit against ABC in 1992 over the network's "PrimeTime Live" show that November, which claimed that Food Lion handled meat and fish in unsanitary ways. The legal battle centers on unaired videotapes allegedly showing the ABC producers pushing Food Lion workers to sell out-of-date merchandise and repackage old meat with new expiration dates after taking jobs at the grocer for an expose. The unaired tape demonstrates "staging," the grocer has charged. McKinley said picture taking was not allowed in the store without the company's permission. "We want to make sure there is a valid reason they want to take the footage," he said. Two producers working at different Food Lion locations wore spy kits -- cameras in their wigs and tape recorders and battery packs under their smocks -- to get the footage. The producers applied for the job under names that did not match the given social security numbers. During testimony, Food Lion lawyer Richard Wyatt asked McKinley about the program's harm to the company. But when an ABC attorney objected to the line of questioning, Tilley sent the jury from the courtroom and said he would not allow testimony on that issue yet. In opening statements, ABC attorney Bill Jeffress denied the two producers had committed fraud but said the company would not contest the allegation that deception had been used. Salisbury, N.C.-based Food Lion, a unit of Belgian retailer Ets Delhaize Freres et Cie LE LION SA, is charging fraud, deceptive trade practices, conspiracy and breach of duty of loyalty against ABC and its producers.
